To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

angiotensin II and its heptapeptide derivative angiotensin (AIII) are potent modulators of nociception and arterial pressure-related responsiveness of neurons in a specific region of the brainstem, the nucleus reticulars gigantocellulars (NRGC).
angiotensin (AIII) modulates the neuronal responsiveness of the NRGC to tail clamp in the presence of elevated arterial pressure, and this effect is receptor-specific.
angiotensin peptides modulate neuronal responsiveness in the NRGC of the medulla to nociception-related input and/or arterial pressure-related input.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the modulation by AIII of the interactive effect on NRGC neuronal responsiveness of noxious stimuli, and elevation in systemic blood pressure.

the possible modulation of the interactive effect on the responsiveness of NRGC neuronal units of the medulla by the neuropeptide AIII of noxious stimuli delivered to the tail and of transient elevation in arterial pressure elicited by the alpha 1-adrenoceptor agonist, phenylephrine.
the modulation of nociception and/or blood pressure-related responsiveness of NRGC cells by the heptapeptidic angiotensin AIII.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
AIII modulates the responsiveness of NRGC to tail clamp and/or phenylephrine-induced hypertension, depending on the prevailing physiologically induced input to the central nervous sytem.
angiotensinergic mechanisms may contribute to the modulation of the responsiveness of NRGC nociceptive neurons in the presence of elevated arterial pressure.
the actions of AIII are complex, and that they are dependent on the prevailing conditions in the central nervous system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
AIII may be involved in the modulation of the central integration of nociception and arterial pressure-related signals.
AIII, in addition to its well-known cardiovascular actions, also exerts a modulating influence on pain-related and cardiovascular-related neuronal responsiveness in NRGC.
the heptapeptides may play an important role in the central modulation of nociceptive information.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain may have evolved a means of modulating neuronal responsiveness in a manner that is dependent upon the nature of the physiologic input to which it is exposed.
the heptapeptide, AIII, can selectively alter the neuronal response to a nociceptive stimulus in a way that favors the nociception-related response over the arterial pressure-related one.

the heptapeptides are likely involved in the integration of cardiovascular and nociceptive signals in the brainstem, and may thus be important in the regulation of cardiovascular reflexes in the face of noxious stimulation.
